ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) -- One of the best gifts you can give a child this holiday season may not be the latest gadget, toy, or tasty treat, but instead the gift of a healthy lifestyle. Participants get a workout at the FitWit fitness boot camp. An Atlanta-based non-profit organization is doing its part to combat childhood obesity by teaching kids proper nutrition and exercise in a six-week fitness boot camp similar to NBC's "The Biggest Loser." The FitWit Foundation hopes its program will catch on nationwide. "We wanted to work with teens in a meaningful way, and we saw firsthand how fitness and physical activity in general is being neglected in this population. With a lot of help from volunteers and donors, we've started a program this past spring that encourages hard work and is a fun way to get in shape," said FitWit instructor Ben Thoele. FitWit's program is a six-week after-school boot camp competition which rewards participants with prizes for meeting fitness goals. An iPod Nano was the grand prize for Atlanta Public Schools students completing a recent fitness session.  Watch for more on FitWit » . Students who are motivated to get in shape but not involved in an organized sports team are selected as contestants. Participants' fitness levels are assessed at the beginning and end of the program. Each week, volunteers lead three 60-minute sessions that include fitness instruction and physical health education. In addition, the participants are assigned two home workouts to be performed between sessions. "After six weeks, all participants have an increased total fitness ability. We averaged over 40 percent improvement in total fitness in our first program last spring. It's common to have a participant double their fitness ability," Thoele said. "A lot of these kids don't know how to work out, or that they even have the capacity to work out. They gain an appreciation for pushing their limits, and when that happens, we see a tremendous boost in their self-confidence," he said. The need for increased fitness across the country is striking. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 17.6 percent of U.S. teenagers were obese in 2006 -- more than triple the rate in 1980.  Obesity puts the teens at increased risk for heart disease, bone and joint problems, sleep apnea, and social and psychological problems, the CDC says. "Success for us is when a kid is thinking about fitness outside of the program, because they enjoy how they feel when they're in better shape," Thoele said. "Our first winner, Raquel, told us that she continued to come because she just felt better. She had incredible numbers as well. She was not able to perform even one sit-up at the start of the program and did 21 in our final assessments. She also shed more than 90 seconds off her mile time." "Since I've been here, I've been eating healthy," one FitWit participant said. "I have been watching what I eat and drink. I drink three cups of water every day. And I exercise more often. I don't spend too much time inside my home anymore."

What sets FitWit's program apart is its thoughtful selection process. # Atlanta, Georgia: The Home of CNN

Atlanta, the capital and most populous city of Georgia, holds a significant place in American media history as the birthplace and headquarters of CNN (Cable News Network). Founded by media entrepreneur Ted Turner in 1980, CNN was the first television channel to provide 24-hour news coverage, forever changing how people around the world consume news.

## Why Atlanta?

Ted Turner chose Atlanta as the base for his groundbreaking network for several strategic reasons. The city offered lower operating costs compared to traditional media hubs like New York City, while still providing access to a major airport and growing telecommunications infrastructure. Atlanta's central location in the southeastern United States also made it a practical hub for national broadcasting.

## CNN Center

The CNN Center, located in downtown Atlanta near Centennial Olympic Park, has served as the network's headquarters for decades. This iconic building not only houses newsrooms and studios but has also become a popular tourist attraction, offering behind-the-scenes tours that allow visitors to see how news is produced and broadcast globally.

## Impact on Atlanta's Identity

CNN's presence has significantly shaped Atlanta's reputation as a major media and business center in the American South. Alongside other prominent companies headquartered in the city—such as Coca-Cola and Delta Air Lines—CNN has helped establish Atlanta as a cosmopolitan hub with global influence, far beyond what might be expected for a city of its size.

## A Lasting Legacy

Even as media consumption habits have evolved with the rise of digital and social platforms, CNN's roots in Atlanta remain a point of civic pride. The network's journalists have covered countless major world events from its Atlanta studios, cementing the city's role not just in Southern culture, but in the broader landscape of global journalism.

Today, "Atlanta, Georgia" is often mentioned in the same breath as CNN, a testament to how one company can become intrinsically linked with the identity of a city.

# Atlanta Nonprofit Puts Teens Through 'Biggest Loser'-Style Boot Camps to Fight Childhood Obesity

**ATLANTA** — On a humid Saturday morning, a group of teenagers gathers in a converted warehouse gym in southwest Atlanta, music thumping as a coach barks encouragement over the sound of jumping jacks and battle ropes. It looks like something out of a reality TV show — and that's precisely the point.

The nonprofit organization Fit Futures Atlanta has spent the past three years running intensive fitness boot camps modeled after the competitive, high-energy format popularized by "The Biggest Loser," but with a mission far removed from prime-time entertainment: combating a childhood obesity crisis that experts say has only worsened since the pandemic.

"We took the parts of that show that actually work — accountability, community, seeing real progress — and left behind the parts that don't, like the shame and the extreme weight-loss timelines," said Marcus Whitfield, the organization's founder and a former college football player who says he struggled with his own weight as a teenager. "This isn't about humiliating kids into losing pounds. It's about giving them tools they'll use for the rest of their lives."

## A Growing Crisis

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, roughly 1 in 5 American children and adolescents is affected by obesity, a rate that has nearly tripled since the 1970s. Georgia consistently ranks among the states with higher-than-average childhood obesity rates, with public health officials pointing to food deserts, limited access to safe recreational spaces, and rising screen time as contributing factors.

Fit Futures Atlanta was born out of Whitfield's frustration watching kids in his own neighborhood lack access to the kind of structured fitness programs wealthier families could afford.

"Gym memberships, personal trainers, sports leagues — that stuff isn't cheap," Whitfield said. "We wanted to build something free, or close to it, that could actually move the needle for families who need it most."

## Inside the Program

The organization's flagship program runs in eight-week cycles, with teens ages 13 to 18 attending sessions three times a week. Each cohort is capped at 20 participants, split into small teams that compete in friendly challenges — obstacle courses, relay races, strength circuits — while also receiving nutrition education and, notably, mental health support.

"We bring in a licensed counselor every single week," said program director Renata Sanchez. "A lot of these kids have complicated relationships with food and their bodies already. We're not trying to add to that. We're trying to undo some of that damage while building healthy habits."

Unlike the dramatic weigh-ins featured on television, Fit Futures avoids public scale sessions altogether. Progress is tracked privately through fitness benchmarks — how far a teen can run, how many push-ups they can complete, energy levels reported through journaling — rather than pounds lost.

"We measure success differently," Sanchez said. "Did a kid go from not being able to run a quarter mile to running two miles? That's a win, regardless of what the scale says."

## Teen Voices

For 16-year-old participant Jayden Coleman, the program has been transformative — though not in the ways he initially expected.

"I thought I was just gonna get in shape," Coleman said, catching his breath after a circuit workout. "But I made friends here. Real friends who check on me. I look forward to coming now. It doesn't feel like punishment."

His mother, Denise Coleman, said she's noticed changes beyond the physical.

"His confidence is different. He stands up straighter. He talks to me about what he's eating without me having to ask," she said. "This program gave him something a lot of these online diet trends never could — community."

## Looking Ahead

Fit Futures Atlanta currently operates out of two locations in the metro area and serves roughly 150 teens annually, funded through a mix of grants, corporate sponsorships, and individual donations. Whitfield said the organization hopes to expand to Savannah and Augusta within the next two years, pending additional funding.

Public health experts caution that community-based programs like Fit Futures, while promising, are not a substitute for broader policy changes — improved school nutrition standards, safer neighborhoods for outdoor activity, and greater access to healthcare.

"Programs like this are incredibly valuable, but they're treating symptoms of a much larger systemic issue," said Dr. Elaine Whitmore, a pediatric health researcher unaffiliated with the nonprofit. "That said, the psychosocial support model they've built — combining fitness with mental health care and avoiding weight-shaming — is genuinely a step in the right direction."

For Whitfield, the mission remains personal.

"I don't want another kid to go through what I went through — the bullying, the low self-esteem, thinking your body defines your worth," he said. "If we can catch that early and give these teens a different relationship with movement and food, we've done our job."

*Fit Futures Atlanta accepts new participants on a rolling basis, with scholarships available for families demonstrating financial need.*

**Community Programs Aim to Curb Rising Childhood Obesity Rates Through Movement and Mentorship**

*By [Staff Writer]*

COLUMBUS, Ohio — On a humid Tuesday evening, a gymnasium at the Eastside Community Center buzzes with the sound of sneakers squeaking against hardwood as a dozen kids run through agility drills. It looks like any other youth sports practice, but the goal here extends beyond athletic skill — organizers say they're fighting a public health crisis one workout at a time.

The program, called Move Forward Youth, is one of a growing number of community-based initiatives across the country designed to address childhood obesity, a condition that continues to affect millions of American children despite decades of public health campaigns.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the obesity rate among children and adolescents ages 2 to 19 stands at approximately 19.7%, affecting about 14.7 million young people nationwide. The rate has nearly tripled since the 1970s, the agency reports, and disparities persist along racial, ethnic and socioeconomic lines. CDC data show obesity prevalence is higher among Hispanic (26.2%) and non-Hispanic Black (24.8%) children compared with their non-Hispanic white (16.6%) and Asian (9.0%) peers.

Health officials warn that childhood obesity is linked to a higher risk of Type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and psychological effects such as anxiety and low self-esteem — conditions that can persist into adulthood if left unaddressed.

"We're not just teaching kids how to do push-ups," said Marcus Reilly, a certified youth fitness instructor who has led the twice-weekly program for the past three years. "We're trying to change their relationship with their own bodies. A lot of these kids have been told their whole lives that something is wrong with them. Our job is to show them what their bodies can actually do."

Reilly, who previously worked as a physical education teacher, said the program blends physical activity with basic nutrition education and mentorship, an approach he believes is more sustainable than diet-focused interventions alone.

"If you just tell a kid to eat less and exercise more, that message doesn't stick," Reilly said. "But if you build community, if you make it fun, if you give them ownership over their health — that's what creates lasting change."

For 13-year-old participant Jaylen Ortiz, the program has meant more than shedding pounds.

"I used to get picked last for everything in gym class," Jaylen said, catching his breath after a drill. "Now I can run the whole session without stopping. My mom says I sleep better too. I actually look forward to coming here — it doesn't feel like a punishment."

Jaylen's mother, Elena Ortiz, said she enrolled her son after his pediatrician raised concerns about his weight during a routine checkup. She credits the program not just with physical improvements but with a noticeable shift in her son's confidence.

"He walks differently now," she said. "He stands up straighter. That's not something a scale measures, but it matters just as much."

Public health experts say programs like Move Forward Youth reflect a broader shift in how communities are approaching obesity prevention — moving away from stigmatizing messaging and toward accessible, judgment-free environments that emphasize long-term habits over short-term results.

Dr. Priya Nandakumar, a pediatrician not affiliated with the program, said community-based interventions can be particularly effective because they address environmental and social factors that clinical settings often cannot.

"A doctor's office visit lasts 15 minutes," Nandakumar said. "These programs give kids sustained, repeated exposure to healthy behaviors in a setting where they feel supported rather than judged. That's incredibly valuable."

Still, experts caution that community programs alone cannot solve a problem rooted in complex factors, including food insecurity, limited access to safe outdoor spaces, and marketing of unhealthy foods to children. The CDC has emphasized that comprehensive strategies — including policy changes in schools, improved access to affordable produce, and urban planning that supports physical activity — are necessary to meaningfully reduce obesity rates nationwide.

For now, organizers of Move Forward Youth say they are focused on the impact they can have locally. The program has grown from eight participants in its first year to more than 40 children currently enrolled, according to Reilly, with a waiting list forming for the fall session.

"We're not going to fix this overnight," Reilly said. "But if a kid leaves here feeling stronger, more confident, and more in control of their health, that's a win. Multiply that by every kid in this gym, and you start to see real change."

As the session wraps up, Jaylen and his teammates line up for a final round of stretches, laughing as they compare how many jumping jacks they can do. For Reilly, moments like these — small, unremarkable, but consistent — are the quiet victories that keep the program running.

"This isn't about a before-and-after photo," he said. "It's about giving these kids tools they'll use for the rest of their lives."

"The holidays can be tough for anyone trying to eat well or stay active," said Maria Chen, the organization's program director. "For teenagers especially, there's so much messaging around food during this season — it's everywhere, from school parties to family gatherings. We wanted to give them tools to enjoy the holidays while still understanding how to take care of their bodies."

## More Than Just a Diet Lesson

The program, which serves roughly 200 teens across three Atlanta-area community centers, doesn't preach restriction. Instead, sessions focus on practical skills: reading nutrition labels, understanding portion sizes, and finding affordable ways to eat vegetables and lean proteins. A hands-on cooking segment has proven particularly popular, where teens learn to recreate healthier versions of holiday classics — like a lower-sugar sweet potato casserole or baked instead of fried sides.

Physical activity components include free weekend fitness sessions at local gyms, partnerships with Atlanta parks for outdoor group workouts, and a "Step Challenge" that gamifies movement over the holiday break, when many teens fall out of their school-year exercise routines.

Sixteen-year-old participant Jaylen Roberts said the program shifted how he thinks about food.

"I used to think eating healthy meant boring meals," Roberts said. "Now I know you can still enjoy holiday food, just make some changes. And I actually like the workouts — it's fun when you're doing it with your friends instead of alone."

## Addressing a Broader Need

Organizers say the timing is intentional. Studies have shown that adolescents often gain weight and lose fitness momentum during the November-to-January stretch, compounded by school breaks, holiday sweets, and reduced outdoor activity in colder months.

Atlanta, like many U.S. cities, has grappled with rising rates of childhood obesity and limited access to nutrition education in under-resourced schools. Fresh Start Atlanta specifically targets neighborhoods where such resources are scarce, partnering with local schools and community centers to identify participants.

"We're not trying to shame anyone about their weight or their family's traditions," Chen emphasized. "We're trying to make sure these kids have knowledge and support systems so they can make informed choices — this holiday season and beyond."

## Looking Ahead

The organization plans to use lessons from this year's holiday programming to expand into a year-round curriculum in local schools by next fall, pending additional grant funding.

For now, Chen said the immediate goal is simple: help teens walk into the new year feeling empowered rather than guilty.

"If a kid leaves one of our sessions and says, 'I know how to make a healthier choice, and I don't feel bad about having pie at Christmas too' — that's success," she said. "That's exactly what we're going for."

---

*Fresh Start Atlanta is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit relying on community donations and volunteer support. More information is available through local community centers in the greater Atlanta area.*
